title: The Welcome
subtitle: Saturday 21 to Sunday 29 September 1974: Free Rooms, Rhubarb Pie, and the Frost That Stopped at the Ridge

setting.name: Hollow Fork, the ridge road and the rim of the Hollow, 21 to 29 September 1974
setting.description: The party's first week in Hollow Fork. Nobody is hostile, nothing attacks, and the town could not be more welcoming: free rooms at the Harvest Moon Motel ('harvest season guests stay on the co-op'), pie at the Fork Diner, invitations to everything, people who remember your name after one meeting. The party is looking for someone: Dawn Petrakis, the hitchhiker who called home from the diner payphone on 8 September; Dr. Howard Gessler, the bowhunter who went into the coulees in October 1973; a pattern of missing travelers; the family that left. The town's answer to every question is kind, consistent and false: Dawn caught the Friday bus west on the 13th; Dr. Gessler must have got lost and gone home some other way, and wasn't his car found in La Crosse; nobody here knows anything about any pattern. This week the party finds out that the answers are false, that Dawn is still here, that the town's luck is not natural, and that everyone knows. On the night of Monday 23 September the killing frost that blackens corn from the Dakotas to Michigan comes over the ridge and stops, exactly, at the ridge road and the creek; on Tuesday the TV van comes for 'the town the frost forgot'. On Sunday 29 September the party is the guest of honour at the Fall Supper in the Community Church basement, and that night the cold comes up out of the Hollow and walks down Main Street for the first time.
setting.atmosphere: Sunlight, maple leaves, coffee, cows and kindness, and under it, small wrong things. Play every townsperson as someone the players would like to have as a neighbour, and let the wrongness come from details: the red kerchiefs knotted at every throat, the hoses running across back steps at night, the conversations that end, the bread in a basket on every table that nobody ever charges for. The Landlord is not seen this week, except as frost and breath and, on the last night, a fog that moves against the wind. The first fear checks are small (DC 10, signs) and the last one is the first real one (DC 15). Let the players eat. Track who does.

keyLocations.name: The Fork Diner
keyLocations.description: A long, bright room on Main Street with a counter and nine stools, six booths along the windows, a pie case, a jukebox with Patsy Cline and Charley Pride on it, a payphone by the door, and a Greyhound schedule taped to the register: westbound to La Crosse and Minneapolis Tuesdays and Fridays at 4:10 p.m., eastbound to Madison and Milwaukee at 11:40 a.m. Elsie Brandvold runs the front; her husband Arvid bakes in the back from four in the morning. The morning coffee crowd (Arnie Fossum, Harald Haugen, Dr. Kubicek, half a dozen farmers in seed caps) sits at the big round table by the window from six to seven. The motel register is kept here, behind the counter, because the co-op owns the motel and Elsie keeps the keys.
features: The bread basket on every table: thick slices of white and rye from Arvid's ovens, wrapped in a cloth printed HOLLOW FORK CO-OP — FROM OUR FIELDS TO YOUR TABLE; it is never on the bill
The payphone by the door, from which Dawn called her sister collect at 7:12 p.m. on Sunday 8 September

The bulletin board: HARVEST DAYS OCT 11-12-13, 70 GOOD YEARS; the Fall Supper sign-up sheet; a Polaroid of the 1973 Harvest Queen; a card for the Kinnick County ASCS office; a FOR SALE notice for a 1968 Farmall
The motel register, a green clothbound book behind the register, and under the counter a cardboard box of old registers back to 1955
A row of red cotton kerchiefs on a nail by the kitchen door, for anybody who forgot theirs
encounters: Elsie Brandvold, 61, who pours coffee before you ask and cuts a second slice before you finish the first
The morning coffee table: Arnie Fossum, Harald Haugen, Dr. Arlen Kubicek and four farmers
Emil Pospisil, the Greyhound driver, at the counter for twelve minutes every Tuesday and Friday afternoon
secrets: CLUE A2 (core, automatic for anyone who reads the register or the old ones in the box): every September since 1955, one guest's line ends with 'checked out' and a date in Elsie's round, generous handwriting, never the guest's; the dates fall between 8 and 20 September; there are nineteen such lines. On this year's page: 'Dawn Petrakis, Rockford Ill., Unit 6, in 8/29, checked out 9/13'. Investigation DC 12: the 'checked out' entries are in a different pen from the rest of each line, added later.

CLUE B2 (core, from Emil Pospisil on a Tuesday or Friday; Persuasion DC 10 or just a cup of coffee and a straight question): no young woman got on his bus at Hollow Fork on Friday 13 September or any day since; nobody gets on at Hollow Fork, hardly ever. He remembers Dawn: she sat at the counter on Tuesday 10 September, asked the fare to Minneapolis ($9.40), said 'maybe after their festival', and gave him a peach out of a paper sack 'the farm lady gave me'. He has driven this route nine years and has noticed, without letting himself think about it, that people get off at Hollow Fork in the fall and do not get back on.

CLUE 1e (the pull): any character born outside Hollow Fork who eats here more than one day running begins to feel it (Rule One; WIS save DC 10, +1 per day): the town seems the most restful place they have ever been, and leaving seems like something that can wait until after the festival. Describe it as a feeling and let the player decide what to do with it.

Elsie's slip, for anyone with Insight DC 13 who asks about Dawn twice: the first time, she says Dawn caught the Friday bus west; the second time, warmly, 'She was going to Minneapolis, the poor thing, I put a sandwich in her bag'; but there is a cardigan of Dawn's (yellow, too big, a Rockford Central High patch on it) on the hook in the kitchen, and when Tess Petrakis sees it Elsie says, too quickly, 'Oh, she left that, you take it to her, I mean, you send it on to her, hon.'

keyLocations.name: The Harvest Moon Motel
keyLocations.description: Eight units in a row at the west end of Main Street, cinder block painted pale green, a gravel lot, a Coke machine and an ice machine that does not work, and behind it a mown yard running down to the north branch of Hollow Fork Creek. The co-op owns it; in harvest season guests stay free. Every room has a chenille bedspread, a Philco television that gets La Crosse, a Bible in the drawer and a framed photograph of the elevator. Dawn stayed in Unit 6 from 29 August to 13 September. Russ Thorsen always gets Unit 3; Elsie keeps it for him.
features: Unit 6: under the drawer of the bedside table, in ballpoint, 'D.P. was here 8/29/74 — Mpls or bust ☮'; a bobby pin in the carpet; the window faces the Hollow
Behind the motel, a garden hose runs from the spigot across the concrete back step and down into the grass, on, all night, every night from mid-September; whoever is on duty turns it on at dusk
The windows: single-glazed, aluminum frames; by the end of the week, frost on the inside
encounters: Elsie or Arvid Brandvold bringing towels, extra blankets and, unasked, a plate of bars
On the night of Monday 23 September, the frost (Act 2)
secrets: CLUE 3a (core, on the night of the frost or any night after for a character sleeping alone with the window shut): the character wakes at about three in the morning cold to the bone; the inside of the window is frosted over, in a fern pattern, except for one patch the size of a face that is clear, as if someone had breathed on it from outside; and then they see that the clear patch is where their own breath has been going all night, and that the frost has formed everywhere else in the room where breath has not, on the mirror, on the TV screen, on the inside of the lampshade. Fear check DC 10. Anyone who watches for a while sees new frost feathering across the glass toward the warm patch, slowly, like something reaching for it, and then retreating when the sun comes up.

CLUE 2c (core, for anyone who goes out back at night or asks about it): the running hose. Arvid, asked, says 'for the frost, keeps the ground from freezing round the foundation', which is nonsense in September and he knows it; every farmhouse a character drives past at night has the same thing, a hose or a hand pump running across the back step. Nature DC 10: running a hose does nothing for frost.

keyLocations.name: Main Street and the Co-op Store
keyLocations.description: Six blocks. The State Bank in red brick with Marit Lunde's office window upstairs; the co-op store (feed, seed, work gloves, overalls, Kools and Winstons, a cooler of pop, a CB radio display, a bulletin board), the co-op office next door with the old Diebold safe visible through the window, the feed mill, and the hundred-and-twenty-foot elevator with HOLLOW FORK CO-OP on it; the Standard station; the village hall and fire house; the Community Church; the Ridge Inn. Pickups with CB whips park diagonally. Everybody wears a red kerchief.
features: The red kerchiefs: knotted at the throat on everyone from the bank president to the boy pumping gas, in the co-op store at 39 cents, 'for Harvest Days, it's tradition'
The CB display in the co-op store, with a hand-lettered card: HOLLOW FORK MONITORS CH. 14 — BREAKER 14 FOR THE CO-OP

Through the co-op office window: Harald Haugen at his desk, a calendar from the Madison bank, and behind him a green steel Diebold safe the size of a refrigerator, painted with gold scrollwork and the date 1903
encounters: Lillian Fossum buying groceries on Tuesdays and Saturdays
Rolf Haugen, 24, driving the co-op's grain truck, the only young person in town who looks as though he is not sleeping well
Marit Lunde, who will offer a character a job (Tess at the clinic, Quentin at the Furrow, Ward hauling for the co-op) by the end of the week
secrets: CLUE B3 (core, for anyone watching the co-op store on a Tuesday or Saturday, or who asks the clerk what Lillian Fossum buys): Lillian buys two packs of Kools every time, and Dawn's brand is Kools (Tess knows, Ward knows; she smoked them in his cab). Nobody at the Fossums' smokes. Insight DC 12 on Lillian: she is frightened, kind, and has not slept. If followed, her Ford pickup goes south out of town to the Fossum place.

CLUE 3c (core, for anyone who asks about the kerchiefs, or who is out at night): at night, in harvest season, townsfolk wet their kerchiefs at the pump and pull them up over their mouths and noses before they go out to the barn. Asked, they laugh: 'Old custom. So the frost doesn't take you for a stranger.' Yolanda Ibarra knows it is recorded nowhere else in the Upper Midwest.

CLUE B4 (core for anyone monitoring channel 14 with a CB, such as Ward's rig; automatic within two evenings): among the talk of drying corn and milk prices, Arnie Fossum's handle, Big Red, and his wife's, Kitchen Window: 'How's our guest?' 'Eating good. Sleeps a lot.' 'You keep her comfortable, now.' Then someone else: 'Breaker one-four, we got ears on this channel, folks,' and the channel goes quiet.

keyLocations.name: The Ridge Road and the Frost Line
keyLocations.description: County Road K climbs east out of the village along the ridge spur to the watershed divide two miles out, then drops toward Linden Falls. From the divide you can see thirty miles of ridges and coulees in every direction. On the morning of Tuesday 24 September, after the killing frost, the view is the strangest thing anyone in the party has ever seen: every field to the east, north and south, over the ridge and across the creek, is black and limp, corn and soybeans and alfalfa scorched by the cold; and every field on Hollow Fork's side is green and gold and untouched, right up to the ditch.
features: At the divide, the frost line runs down the middle of County Road K: the east ditch grass is black and stiff with frost, the west ditch grass is green and wet with dew
Along the creek, the line follows the far bank exactly
The La Crosse TV station's news van, a white Ford Econoline with CHANNEL 8 ACTION NEWS on the side and a mast on top, parked at the divide on Tuesday morning with a reporter doing her stand-up
encounters: Bonnie Sedlak, the TV reporter, and Xavier Boone, her cameraman, filming 'the town the frost forgot'
A farmer from over the ridge, Ed Rasmussen, standing in his black corn looking across the road at the Fossums' green, saying nothing
secrets: CLUE 2a (core, automatic at the divide or along the creek on Tuesday morning; fear check DC 10 for anyone who walks the line and understands it): the frost stopped where Hollow Fork's water stops. A character who walks along the line for half a mile sees that it does not follow a fence or a property line or the lie of the land; it follows the crest of the ridge exactly, and the creek banks exactly. Nature DC 13: it is following the watershed divide. Ed Rasmussen, asked, says only: 'Hail does the same. Every time. My dad said so and his dad said so. We don't talk about it.'
Xavier Boone, the cameraman, films the line from the van mast and says to nobody in particular, 'That isn't weather.' He is a possible companion from this point on.

keyLocations.name: The Rim of the Hollow and the Stone House
keyLocations.description: South of the village, past the Fossum place, a farm lane runs between walls of standing corn to the rim of the Hollow. There, on the lip of the coulee, stands a small fieldstone house with a slate roof and a lilac hedge, the oldest house in the township: Ingeborg Vaage's. From her yard the land drops two hundred feet into a wooded coulee; across it, on a bench at the head of the Hollow, the Old Union Church, grey and sagging, its steeple leaning; below the church, a slope of mossy broken rock, and at its foot, half hidden by birches, a low dark opening. On a warm afternoon, cold air flows up over the rim and pools in Ingeborg's yard, smelling of wet stone, and her lilacs are still green when everyone else's have dropped their leaves.
features: Ingeborg's yard: a hand pump by the back step, running into a stone trough and overflowing into a ditch, all day and all night
The rim: crows, dozens, in the oaks; they do not caw
The Cold Hole, visible from the rim with field glasses: frost furring its lip in September sunlight, and every so often, a breath of white vapour out, and then, slowly, the vapour drawn back in
encounters: Ingeborg Vaage, 82, in a cardigan and gumboots, with a cup of coffee for anyone who comes up the lane
A Crow Swarm (Crow Swarm stats) if anyone climbs down past the rim, which nobody in town would do
secrets: Ingeborg's warning (core, for anyone who visits her and is kind; she knows who they are before they say): she will not talk about the Hollow, the bargain or the town; she talks about her lilacs, her late husband and the year the elevator was built. But when they leave, she says: 'You've eaten our bread. You should go home now, before you're asked to stay.' Insight DC 10: she means it, and it costs her to say it.

CLUE 3e (for a Sensitive using The Thin Place at the rim, or anyone who stands at the rim at dusk and listens; fear check DC 15 for the Sensitive, who feels it fully): something enormous, below, tasting the air; not looking, because it cannot look; breathing in, slowly, and stopping, as if it had noticed one breath among many. The strongest emotion soaked into the rim is not fear. It is patience.
The Thin Place at the stone house: grief, seventy years of it, and gratitude, and guilt, all at once, so thick it is like walking into wet wool.

synopsis: The party arrives in Hollow Fork on Saturday 21 September, each for their own reason, and finds a town that welcomes them like family: free rooms, pie, coffee, an invitation to the Fall Supper and the seventieth Harvest Days. Over the week they discover three things. First, that travelers have been vanishing from Hollow Fork in September and October for a very long time: Quentin Talbert's list of missing-persons reports, the motel register where one guest every September has been 'checked out' in Elsie Brandvold's handwriting for nineteen years, and Russ Thorsen's client, Dr. Gessler, who disappeared here last October. Second, that Dawn Petrakis never left: the Greyhound driver says no one got on, Dawn's postcard to her sister is postmarked three days after she supposedly left, Lillian Fossum buys Dawn's brand of cigarettes, and channel 14 asks after 'our guest'. Third, that something unnatural keeps Hollow Fork's luck: on the night of 23 September a killing frost blackens the whole Upper Midwest and stops exactly at Hollow Fork's watershed, and frost forms on the inside of the motel windows reaching for the sleepers' breath; everyone wears a red kerchief they wet and pull over their mouths at night; every back step has a hose running across it. Ingeborg Vaage, the oldest woman in town, tells them to go home before they are asked to stay. At the Fall Supper on Sunday 29 September the town feeds them, toasts them and asks them to stay for Harvest Days, and that night the cold comes up out of the Hollow and walks down Main Street, frosting the streetlights, breathing, and the party sees it for the first time. The scenario ends with the party knowing that Dawn is somewhere in Hollow Fork, alive, that the whole town is keeping a secret, and that the secret is in the Hollow.
hook: Each pregen's sheet gives a reason to be on Main Street on Saturday 21 September. Tess Petrakis has a postcard from her sister postmarked Hollow Fork, 16 September. Ward Mrozek is the trucker who dropped Dawn off. Russ Thorsen has come back, as he has every month for a year, to look for his client. Quentin Talbert has a list. Yolanda Ibarra has a reservation for Harvest Days and a 1904 newspaper clipping. Sylvie Aldahl has her grandmother's photograph and her grandmother's warning. They meet at the diner, where Elsie seats strangers together in the big booth because 'you all look like you could use the company'.

conclusions.conclusion: A. Travelers vanish from Hollow Fork every harvest
clues: A1: Quentin Talbert's list of eleven missing-persons reports in twenty years, all last placed in Kinnick County in September or October (Quentin's notebook; or the wire morgue)
A2: the motel registers: one guest every September 'checked out' in Elsie's hand (the Fork Diner)
A3: Dr. Howard Gessler, October 1973, his car found at the La Crosse bus depot with his bow case still in the trunk (Russ Thorsen; the sheriff's report in hs-scenario-002)
Ingeborg Vaage's 'before you're asked to stay' (the stone house)

conclusions.conclusion: B. Dawn never left Hollow Fork; somebody is keeping her
clues: B1: Dawn's postcard to Tess postmarked Hollow Fork 16 September, three days after she 'caught the Friday bus' (Tess's handbag)
B2: Emil Pospisil, the Greyhound driver: nobody got on (the diner, Tuesday or Friday)
B3: Lillian Fossum buys two packs of Kools every time (the co-op store)
B4: 'How's our guest? Eating good' on channel 14 (any CB)
Elsie's slip about Dawn's cardigan (the diner kitchen)

conclusions.conclusion: C. Something that is not natural keeps Hollow Fork's luck, and the whole town knows
clues: 2a: the frost line along the watershed, and the hail that does the same (the ridge road, Tuesday)
3a: frost on the inside of the motel windows, reaching for the sleeper's breath (the motel)
3c: the red kerchiefs, wetted and pulled over the mouth at night (Main Street)
2c: the hoses running across every back step all night (the motel, the farms)
4e: Signe Aldahl's photograph of seven men at the rim of the Hollow in 1904 (Sylvie's handbag)
1e: the pull, felt by any outsider who keeps eating the town's bread (the diner)

acts.title: Saturday and Sunday: The Welcome
acts.description: The party arrives and is welcomed. The point of this act is to make Hollow Fork a real place full of people the players like, to bring the pregens together at one table, and to plant the first wrong notes. Nobody refuses to talk. Everybody lies, kindly, with the same story. Let the players eat, and note who does.
objectives: Meet each other in the big booth at the Fork Diner and compare reasons for being here
Ask after Dawn Petrakis (or Dr. Gessler) and hear the town's story: she caught the Friday bus on the 13th
Look at the motel register, Unit 6 and the Greyhound schedule

scenes.name: Pie at the Fork Diner
scenes.description: Saturday, 4:15 p.m. The Greyhound pulls out westbound and the party, however they arrived, ends up in the diner. Elsie seats strangers together in the big booth by the jukebox, brings coffee and the bread basket without asking, and talks: the weather, the frost warnings on the radio ('not here, hon, never here'), the seventieth Harvest Days, the parade, the pie auction, the TV people coming. Each pregen has a question; Elsie has an answer for every one. Dawn? 'Oh, that sweet girl from Rockford. She was here two weeks, helped me with the dishes, and she caught the Friday bus west on the thirteenth. Minneapolis. I put a sandwich in her bag.' Dr. Gessler? 'Your doctor fellow, Russ? Oh, honey. We all looked. You know we all looked.' The 1904 Harvest Supper? 'Well, that was the first one. Seventy years!' The coffee table by the window listens and smiles. Harald Haugen comes over to shake hands, introduces himself as the co-op manager and tells them their rooms are on the co-op. Arnie Fossum asks Ward if that's his Kenworth by the elevator and offers to have the boys look at a leaking air line. This is the scene where the players meet each other: let them talk.
scenes.readAloud: The Fork Diner smells of coffee, fried onions and something baking. The booths are red vinyl, the counter is chrome and Formica, and the jukebox is playing Patsy Cline to a room that is nearly full on a Saturday afternoon: farmers in seed caps and feed-store jackets, two old women sharing a slice of pie, a teenage boy in a letter jacket, a family with three little kids drawing on the placemats. Every one of them has a red kerchief knotted at the throat. A woman of sixty in a blue apron, round, quick and smiling, takes one look at you and says, "Well, you're not from here, and you look like you've had a long day. Sit, sit. That big booth. I'll bring coffee." She brings coffee, and cream, and a basket of thick-sliced bread wrapped in a cloth that says HOLLOW FORK CO-OP — FROM OUR FIELDS TO YOUR TABLE, and a slice of rhubarb pie for each of you that you did not order. "On the house. First time in Hollow Fork, first slice is on the house. That's the rule." Behind her, through the round window in the kitchen door, a big grey-haired man in a baker's cap lifts his floury hand in a wave. Outside, across the street, the banner moves in the breeze: 70 GOOD YEARS.

skillChecks.success: Elsie is telling a story she has told before, and she believes the part about the sandwich. She is not afraid of you. She is sad about something, deep down, and she is fond of you already, which is the strangest part. Every time someone at the coffee table laughs, Harald Haugen does not.
skillChecks.failure: Elsie is the friendliest woman you have ever met, and the pie is extraordinary.

skillChecks.success: Nobody here pays for bread. Nobody here is without a kerchief. Nobody here has asked any of you why you came. And the payphone by the door has a little card taped above it in Elsie's round hand: LOCAL CALLS 10¢ — LONG DISTANCE SEE ELSIE.
skillChecks.failure: It is a busy, friendly little diner. The jukebox plays Charley Pride next.

skillChecks.success: Elsie lets you look at the motel register "since you're worried, hon", and shows you Dawn's line: in 8/29, checked out 9/13. If you ask about older years she says there's a box of the old ones under the counter "going back to Eisenhower" and laughs, and lets you look while she does the dishes. (CLUE A2.)
skillChecks.failure: Elsie pats your hand and says that Dawn was a grown woman with her own mind, and these young people do just go, don't they. She refills your coffee and goes to the kitchen, and when she comes back she has brought you more bread.

scenes.name: Unit 6
scenes.description: The Harvest Moon Motel. Elsie gives the party keys to adjoining units and sends Arvid over with extra blankets. Dawn's old room, Unit 6, is empty and clean; Elsie lets them in if asked. Russ gets Unit 3, as always, and Elsie has already turned down his bed. Tonight, and every night, someone turns on the hose behind the motel at dusk. Anyone awake late sees, across the road, the lights of the Fossum farmhouse a mile south, and beyond it the dark of the Hollow, and hears the grain dryers roaring all night on the farms. Any player who wants to sit up and watch sees nothing more on this first night than a pickup that drives slowly past at midnight, and a woman's figure, Elsie, crossing from the diner to check that the hose is running.
scenes.readAloud: Unit 6 is like the others: pale green walls, a chenille spread, a Philco TV on a stand, a painting of the elevator at sunset, a window facing south across a mown yard to the creek, and beyond the creek, rows of corn running to a line of dark trees. Somebody has cleaned it carefully, recently. The bedside drawer sticks; when you pull it all the way out, there is writing on the underside of the table, in blue ballpoint, small and neat: D.P. was here 8/29/74 — Mpls or bust, and a peace sign. Out back, as the light goes, someone has turned on a garden hose. It lies across the concrete step and runs down into the grass, and the water whispers there in the dark, and keeps whispering.

skillChecks.success: The 'checked out' entries in the registers are in a different pen from the rest of each line, added later; nineteen of them, one a year since 1955, each between 8 and 20 September. Dawn's is one. And Dawn's line in this year's register has, in the margin, a tiny pencilled tick that the other guests' lines do not have; so do each of the nineteen.
skillChecks.failure: The registers are what they look like: twenty years of salesmen, hunters and visiting relatives.

skillChecks.success: Under the bed, wedged in the frame, a matchbook from the Ridge Inn with a phone number written inside in a girl's hand: Tess's number, in Rockford. And from the window: the hose is not the only one. Every farmhouse light you can see has, if you watch long enough, someone come out at dusk and do something at the back step.
skillChecks.failure: A clean motel room with nothing in it. Whoever cleaned it was thorough.

skillChecks.success: A hose running all night does nothing for frost in September, nothing for a foundation and nothing for a lawn that is already soaked. Whatever it is for, it is not for anything that grows. (CLUE 2c.)
skillChecks.failure: Farm people have their ways. Maybe it is for the frost.

scenes.name: Channel 14
scenes.description: Ward Mrozek's Kenworth has a forty-channel Cobra CB in the cab; Russ's pickup has a cheaper one; the co-op store sells them. Hollow Fork talks on channel 14: corn moisture, milk prices, who is drying tonight, whose cows are out, a ball game. Anyone who monitors for two evenings hears the Fossums (CLUE B4). Ward can break in and chat as Polecat; the farmers are friendly to a trucker. Deception DC 12 to ask a leading question without the channel closing. If the party ever talks about Dawn on 14, the town hears it, and the attitude moves to Concerned.
scenes.readAloud: The CB hisses and pops. Somebody is drying corn and wants to know if the co-op has propane on Monday. Somebody's heifers are out on K again. "Big Red, Big Red, you got your ears on?" "Yeah, go ahead, Kitchen Window." "Bringing the casserole over to the church at six." "Ten-four. How's our guest?" A pause. "Eating good. Sleeps a lot." "You keep her comfortable, now." Another voice, older, flat: "Breaker one-four. We got ears on this channel, folks." And the channel goes quiet, all of it, all at once, the way a room goes quiet when the wrong person walks in.

skillChecks.success: You rig the cab radio with a longer whip and a scanner crystal; from now on you can monitor channel 14 from the motel lot, and you will catch anything said on it after dark. The old flat voice that closed the channel is a base station, not a mobile: a big antenna. It is on the co-op elevator.
skillChecks.failure: You hear what anyone hears, when you happen to be listening.

skillChecks.success: As a friendly trucker laid over for the festival, you get Big Red chatting about the harvest, his new barn, his boys, the four hundred acres he bought last year "at six hundred an acre, God help me". He is a nice man, proud and worried. He never says another word about a guest.
skillChecks.failure: The farmers are friendly and talk about nothing. After a while someone says, pleasantly, "Polecat, you're a long way off your route," and nobody answers you again that night.

skillChecks.success: Kitchen Window is a woman trying to sound normal and not managing it. Big Red is a man who has decided not to think about something. The flat voice is a man who has carried a weight for a very long time.
skillChecks.failure: Farm talk. A casserole. Somebody's guest.

encounters: None hostile. The Ridge Inn on Saturday night offers a friendly drunk farmer, Gordy Lien (Frightened Townsman stats if it matters), who tells a stranger that 'Hollow Fork takes care of its own' and then, unprompted, that they should wet their kerchief before they walk home, and buys them a beer

acts.title: Monday to Wednesday: The Frost
acts.description: The killing frost. On Monday 23 September the radio warns of a hard freeze across the Upper Midwest. That night it comes, and stops at the ridge. The point of this act is the first undeniable sign that Hollow Fork's luck is not natural, and the first sign that something is interested in the party. It is also the week the TV van and the Greyhound bring outsiders who can be allies.
objectives: Survive the night of the frost and see what the frost does inside the motel
See the frost line at the ridge and the creek, and understand that it follows the water
Talk to Emil Pospisil, the Greyhound driver, on Tuesday afternoon
Meet the TV crew, Bonnie Sedlak and Xavier Boone

scenes.name: Breath on the Glass
scenes.description: The night of Monday 23 September. Run it room by room for any character sleeping alone with the window shut (CLUE 3a): they wake at three in the morning, cold to the bone, to frost on the inside of the glass and everywhere in the room except where their breath has gone. Fear check DC 10. Anyone who stays awake and watches sees the frost feathering across the glass toward their breath, slowly, retreating when they move or speak, then coming again. Anyone who goes outside sees a white ground fog lying along the creek behind the motel and not crossing the running hose; it lies in a long bank exactly at the edge of the water's wet, like snow against a fence. Anyone who walks into the fog (nobody should) feels a cold that hurts, and hears, very close, a long, slow inhalation; fear check DC 15; Frost Touch (campaign controlFile) if they stay. At first light the fog is gone, and the hose is still running, and Elsie is on the back step with a cup of coffee looking at the corn, which is green.
scenes.readAloud: You wake because you are cold. Not chilly: cold, the way a lake is cold, in your hands and your teeth. The room is grey with the first light from the window, and the window is white. Frost has grown over the inside of the glass in ferns and feathers, thick as a fingernail, except for one round patch the size of a face, right where your head lies on the pillow, through which you can see the dark yard. It takes you a moment to understand that the clear patch is where your own breath has been going all night. Then you see the mirror, white. The TV screen, white. The inside of the lampshade, white. Frost on everything in the room that your breath has not touched. As you watch, very slowly, a new feather of frost creeps out across the glass toward the warm round patch, reaching, and stops, and draws back, when you breathe out.

skillChecks.success: You have read of frost that reaches and of things that hunt by breath, though never both together; whatever is outside cannot see the room, only feel the warmth in it, and it was not trying to come in. It was tasting. Knowing that lowers this fear check's DC by 2 for you, if you have not rolled it yet.
skillChecks.failure: There is no story you know that fits this. That is worse.

skillChecks.success: Out the back window, in the grey: a bank of white ground fog lies along the creek and up the yard, and it stops in a straight edge exactly where the hose water has wetted the grass. It does not cross. It moves, a little, along the line, the way a dog moves along a fence.
skillChecks.failure: There is fog in the yard. It is gone by sunrise.

skillChecks.success: Room by room: everyone who slept with the window shut has the same frost; anyone who slept with a window open, or in a car, or with the heat on, does not. The motel's thermometer by the office door reads 41°F. It was not cold enough outside for frost.
skillChecks.failure: It was a cold night. Old motels are drafty.

scenes.name: The Town the Frost Forgot
scenes.description: Tuesday morning. The radio says the frost has killed corn from the Dakotas to Michigan. The party, driving anywhere, sees the line (CLUE 2a). At the divide on County Road K the Channel 8 news van is filming: Bonnie Sedlak, 33, sharp, ambitious, looking for a story she can take to Minneapolis, and Xavier Boone, 29, her cameraman, Vietnam veteran, quiet, who has just filmed the line from the van mast and does not like it. Ed Rasmussen, a farmer from over the ridge, stands in his black field looking across the road at green corn. Bonnie interviews whoever looks interesting, the party included; Marit Lunde arrives in her Buick to give Bonnie a statement about 'Hollow Fork's careful farming and good drainage' and to invite Channel 8 back to broadcast live from Harvest Days. Bonnie accepts. Xavier, if anyone talks to him straight, says: 'I've seen a lot of things from a helicopter. I've never seen weather follow a map.'
scenes.readAloud: At the top of the ridge, where County Road K crosses the divide, the world splits in two. To the east, as far as you can see, over thirty miles of ridges and coulees, every field is black: corn hanging limp and dark as if it had been boiled, soybeans shrivelled, the alfalfa grey, a whole country killed in one night. To the west, behind you, Hollow Fork's fields are green and gold in the morning sun, tasselled corn rustling, a man on a tractor already chopping silage. The line between them runs down the middle of the road. You can stand with one boot on frozen black grass and one on green grass wet with dew. A white news van is parked on the shoulder with a mast up and a camera on it, and a woman in a camel coat is talking into a microphone, and fifty yards away, in the black field on the east side, an old farmer stands with his hands in his pockets, looking across the road at the green, and does not move.

skillChecks.success: Walk the line half a mile either way and it is unmistakable: it is not following a fence or a slope or a frost pocket. It follows the crest of the watershed divide exactly, and where the creek comes in, it follows the far bank exactly. Whatever stopped the frost is bounded by Hollow Fork's water. (CLUE 2a.)
skillChecks.failure: A frost line, sharp as a knife. You have never seen one like it. You do not know what it means.

skillChecks.success: Ed Rasmussen talks, a little: 'Hail does the same. Comes up the valley black as your hat and splits at the ridge like a creek round a rock. My dad said so and his dad said so. Insurance man's got a map. We don't talk about it, over here. They're good neighbours. They'd give you the shirt off their back.' And then: 'My uncle went to work for Haugen's co-op in '51. They had a bad year that year. Only one.'
skillChecks.failure: The old farmer says he has nothing to say to TV people, and nothing to say to anyone from Hollow Fork, and goes back to his house.

skillChecks.success: Bonnie Sedlak smells a story and does not care whether it is a weather story or something else. Xavier Boone is frightened, and is the kind of man who goes toward what frightens him. Marit Lunde, giving her statement about drainage, is lying, and lying well, and does not want the TV here at all; somebody else invited them and she is making the best of it.
skillChecks.failure: The TV people want a nice story. The banker gives them one.

scenes.name: The Tuesday Bus
scenes.description: Tuesday 24 September, 3:58 p.m., the westbound Greyhound pulls up outside the Fork Diner for its twelve-minute stop; again on Friday 27th. Emil Pospisil, 52, a big, sad, decent man from La Crosse, has his coffee and doughnut at the counter. He gives CLUE B2 to anyone who asks a straight question. If asked about other years, he is silent for a while, and then says he has noticed people getting off at Hollow Fork in the fall and not getting back on, and has told himself they had cars waiting. He will carry a letter, a roll of film or a person out of town for anyone who asks, and from this point on he is a friend; in hs-scenario-004, when the town cancels the Friday stop, he comes anyway. Meanwhile Tess's postcard (CLUE B1) can be compared with the bus timetable: postmarked Hollow Fork 16 September, a Monday, three days after Dawn 'caught the Friday bus'.
scenes.readAloud: The Greyhound comes up Main Street at two minutes to four with its sign reading LA CROSSE - MINNEAPOLIS and stops with a long sigh of air brakes outside the diner. Nobody gets off. Nobody is waiting to get on. The driver climbs down, a heavy man in a grey uniform with a face like a tired bloodhound, and comes into the diner, and Elsie has a cup of coffee and a cake doughnut on the counter for him before the door has shut behind him. "Emil." "Elsie." He sits and eats and looks at nothing, the way a man does who drives the same road twice a week and has stopped seeing it.

skillChecks.success: Emil tells you about the girl with the peach (CLUE B2), and that nobody got on here on the thirteenth, and then, looking at his coffee: 'People get off here in the fall. Salesmen. Kids hitching. A hunter or two. I don't remember picking many of them up again. I figured they had cars.' He writes his home phone number on a napkin.
skillChecks.failure: Emil says he has a schedule to keep and doesn't remember every passenger. But he looks at you while he says it, and at Elsie, and back at you.

skillChecks.success: Dawn's postcard (a photo of the elevator: GREETINGS FROM HOLLOW FORK, WIS.) is postmarked HOLLOW FORK WIS SEP 16 1974. It says: 'Tessie: I'm sorry about the money. I'm staying a while! Mrs. F needs help with the harvest cooking, room and board and $2 an hour, and the people here are SO nice. There's a festival. Don't be angry. Love you. D. P.S. Tell Polecat thanks for the ride.' (CLUE B1.) The writing is Dawn's, but loose and loopy, as though she wrote it half asleep.
skillChecks.failure: A postcard from a girl who is happy where she is.

skillChecks.success: Elsie, watching you talk to Emil, is not angry. She looks the way a mother looks when a child has found out about Santa Claus.
skillChecks.failure: Elsie is busy at the grill.

encounters: The fog behind the motel on the night of the 23rd: not a fight; the Landlord's Frost Touch (campaign controlFile) for anyone foolish enough to walk into it, and a fear check DC 15

acts.title: Thursday to Sunday: Neighbors
acts.description: The party follows the threads to the Fossum place and the stone house at the rim, and the town, now Concerned, keeps them close: jobs offered, invitations, a fixed air line on Ward's rig, Dr. Kubicek dropping in at the motel to see if anyone needs anything. The act ends with the Fall Supper on Sunday 29 September, the town's warmest scene, and the night walk home when the party sees the cold for the first time.
objectives: Follow Lillian Fossum and find where she goes
Visit Ingeborg Vaage at the stone house on the rim, and look into the Hollow
Attend the Fall Supper, and survive the walk home

scenes.name: Kools at the Co-op Store
scenes.description: Thursday or Saturday. Lillian Fossum, 46, comes in for groceries and two packs of Kools (CLUE B3). Watching or following her takes the party to the Fossum place south of town: a white farmhouse, a big new free-stall dairy barn, three Harvestore silos, two farm dogs, three teenage sons, and across the yard a small white hired man's house with its curtains drawn, where on a sunny afternoon a young woman with long dark hair sits on the step in a too-big cardigan, smoking, with her eyes half shut, while Lillian brings her a tray. This is Dawn. The party can see her from the road with field glasses (Perception DC 12) or by sneaking up through the windbreak (Stealth DC 13; the dogs, Feral Dog stats but farm dogs, bark rather than bite unless cornered, and nobody should hurt them). If the party goes to the door now, Lillian, white-faced, says Dawn is sick with a bad flu and Dr. Kubicek says no visitors, and Arnie and two of his sons come out of the barn; the town moves to Watchful. GM: the better play for the town is that the party only glimpses her this week. In hs-scenario-002 they come back.
scenes.readAloud: The woman at the co-op checkout is in her forties, tall, tired, in a barn coat with a red kerchief at her throat, and she is buying the groceries of a farm family of five, a sack of flour, ten pounds of hamburger, Wonder bread, two gallons of milk though she must have a barn full of it, and, at the end, quietly, two packs of Kools from the rack behind the counter. The clerk rings them up without comment, the way he has rung them up before. She takes her change, and her hand is shaking, and she sees you see it. She smiles at you, a good, warm, terrified smile, and says, "Harvest season. Never enough hours in the day," and goes out to a blue Ford pickup and drives south.

skillChecks.success: Through the windbreak and up to the corner of the corn crib without the dogs giving you away: across the yard, on the step of the little white house, a young woman with long dark hair, in a yellow-trimmed cardigan, smoking a menthol with her eyes half shut, the way someone sits in the sun after a long illness. She looks content. She looks like someone who has been asleep for a month and would like to go back to sleep. Lillian comes out with a tray, a bowl of soup and bread, and sits with her, and strokes her hair. (If Tess or Ward is there: it is Dawn.)
skillChecks.failure: The dogs find you before you are halfway through the windbreak, barking fit to wake the dead, and Arnie Fossum comes out of the barn with a pitchfork, sees you, and puts it down, and says, pleasantly, "You folks lost? The motel's back up the road." The town moves to Concerned, if it was not already.

skillChecks.success: From the road with field glasses: the hired man's house has its curtains drawn on a sunny day; a hose runs across its back step, and a second one across the front. Someone has hung a red kerchief on its door knob. And on the step, for a minute, a young woman with long dark hair comes out to smoke.
skillChecks.failure: A big dairy farm on a working afternoon: cows, boys, dogs, a tractor, corn to the horizon.

skillChecks.success: Lillian Fossum is the most frightened person you have met in Hollow Fork, and the kindest. Whatever is going on, she is doing it with her whole heart and hating every minute. She would help you if she thought there was any way to do it and keep her boys safe.
skillChecks.failure: A busy farm wife at harvest time.

scenes.name: The Stone House at the Rim
scenes.description: The farm lane past the Fossum place ends at Ingeborg Vaage's stone house on the rim of the Hollow. Ingeborg, 82, sharp, small, gumboots, a cardigan and a red kerchief, has coffee on and knows exactly who the party are (she has a CB too). She talks about anything but the Hollow: her lilacs, her late husband Leif, the elevator going up in 1949, the polio summer the town didn't have. Sylvie Aldahl, if present, she recognises at once: 'You have Signe's eyes. She was my friend. Tell me she was happy, over there.' She gives the warning as they leave. From her yard the party can see the Hollow, the Old Union Church at its head and the Cold Hole below. The Sensitive's Thin Place here gives CLUE 3e. If the party asks to go down into the Hollow, Ingeborg says, flatly, 'Not this year,' and nothing else; and nobody in Hollow Fork will go with them.
scenes.readAloud: The lane runs between walls of standing corn taller than a man, and then the corn stops and there is nothing in front of you but air. The land falls away two hundred feet into a coulee full of trees, oaks and maples gone red and gold, and among them, oddly, the white trunks of birches and the dark spires of firs, as if a piece of the north woods had been dropped in here. At the head of the coulee, on a bench of land, a grey wooden church leans, its steeple crooked. Below it, a slope of broken mossy rock, and at its foot, a dark low opening, and around the opening, white, in the September sun, frost. As you watch, a breath of white vapour comes out of it, slowly, and hangs, and then, slowly, is drawn back in. Cold air flows over the rim and over your shoes like water. In the oaks along the rim, there are crows, a great many crows, and not one of them makes a sound. Behind you a small fieldstone house sits in its lilacs, and an old woman on the step is holding out a cup of coffee.

skillChecks.success: Ingeborg does not tell you anything about the Hollow. But she tells you, apropos of nothing, that she was twelve years old in the summer of 1904, and her mother was dying of the fever, and her father went out one night and came back at dawn, and her mother sat up in bed that morning and asked for coffee, and lived to be ninety. 'And that is all I will say to strangers, and more than I should.'
skillChecks.failure: Ingeborg talks about lilacs and the elevator and her husband for an hour, and is lovely company, and tells you nothing. As you go: 'You've eaten our bread. You should go home now, before you're asked to stay.'

skillChecks.success: A cold-air slope and an ice cave are natural things, you know that; there are dozens in the Driftless. But the breath of this one is wrong: it goes in as well as out, at a sleeper's rhythm, and the crows are not roosting, they are keeping their distance. Whatever is down there is not a spirit of a dead person; there is no grief in it. It is older than that, and it wants something, and it is waiting.
skillChecks.failure: An ice cave in a coulee. It is very beautiful and you do not want to go down there.

skillChecks.success: Behind the Old Union Church, in the long grass of the old settlers' cemetery, there is a neat row of small fieldstones, newer than the graves, many of them, laid in a line along the fence. Someone mows around them. From here you can't count them. (They are for hs-scenario-002.)
skillChecks.failure: A sagging old church, a cemetery gone to grass, a cave mouth breathing.

scenes.name: The Fall Supper
scenes.description: Sunday 29 September, six o'clock, the Community Church basement. Pastor Tove Hagstrom, 31, the new pastor since June, welcomes the party at the door; she is an outsider too, warm, funny, a little lonely, and genuinely glad of some new faces. The whole town is there: long tables, folding chairs, Jell-O salads, hotdish, ham, scalloped potatoes, a hundred pies, and in the middle of every table a basket of Arvid's bread. The party is seated at the head table as guests of honour. Harald Haugen gives a short, halting welcome and raises a glass of coffee 'to our guests'. Marit Lunde invites them to stay for Harvest Days. Arnie Fossum tells a funny story. Dr. Kubicek asks Tess about nursing. Elsie fills plates. It is the warmest room the players will be in all campaign, and every outsider who eats here is fed by the whole town at once (Rule One). Pastor Tove, at some point, says to whoever she trusts most: 'They've been so good to me. Sometimes I feel like I've been adopted. Sometimes I feel like I'm being fattened.' And laughs. Then the walk home, about nine o'clock, through the dark village: the fog comes up Main Street from the south, out of the Hollow, against the wind, frosting the streetlights one by one, and stops at the diner's hose, and turns, and comes along the street toward whoever is outside. Fear check DC 15. It is the first time they see it. Townsfolk walking home pull up their wet kerchiefs, step briskly onto the nearest running hose's wet, and wait, calm, for it to pass. It does not take anyone tonight. It is not time. It passes close enough that a character feels it breathe in, beside their face.
scenes.readAloud: The cold comes up Main Street from the south like a tide coming in. First you notice that your breath is smoking. Then the streetlight at the end of the block, by the bank, goes dim, and then white, frosting over in a second as if someone had breathed on it, and then the next one, and the next, coming closer. Under them, filling the street from curb to curb, a low white fog is moving toward you at a walking pace, against the wind; the wind is in your face from the north and the fog is coming from the south. It makes no sound, except, as it gets closer, a long, slow intake of breath, like a sleeper about to wake, so deep and so slow it seems to go on for a minute. Around you, the people of Hollow Fork walking home from supper, the old couple with the pie plates, the family with the sleeping baby, a teenager with a guitar case, do not run. They pull their red kerchiefs up over their mouths and noses, and step, calmly, onto the wet concrete where the diner's hose is running across the sidewalk, and stand very still, and wait for it to pass.

skillChecks.success: At the supper: everyone here loves you a little, and is sorry for you a little, and none of them will look at you when Harald says 'to our guests'. Lillian Fossum leaves early, crying, and her husband goes after her. Pastor Tove notices too, and does not know what she has noticed.
skillChecks.failure: The best church supper you have ever been to. Somebody puts a second piece of pie on your plate.

skillChecks.success: You do what the townsfolk do, or something like it: hold your breath, cover your mouth, keep still on the wet. The fog flows past you so close it frosts your eyelashes, and stops, and hangs there, breathing in, and goes on up the street, and over the creek it cannot go, and back down toward the Hollow. It passed you by. (A demonstration of Rule Three, if the players are paying attention.)
skillChecks.failure: Your breath smokes in the cold, a white plume in the frosted light, and the fog stops beside you, and turns, and you feel it breathe in, the warmth pulled out of your mouth and throat like a thread out of a sleeve. Frost Touch (controlFile): 3d8 cold, CON save DC 14 or restrained until the end of your next turn; then someone pulls you onto the wet concrete, and it goes on. It is not time, yet.

skillChecks.success: The fog stops at every running hose like a dog at a fence, and at the creek it stops dead. It went past every townsperson without pausing. It paused at every one of you.
skillChecks.failure: The fog comes, and goes, and you are on the wet sidewalk shaking, and Elsie has her arm around you and is saying, 'There, there. It's just the weather. It's just the weather, hon.'

encounters: The Fossums' two farm dogs (Feral Dog stats; they bark and hold ground, and a sensible party does not hurt them)
A Crow Swarm if anyone goes down past the rim of the Hollow
The Landlord on Main Street after the Fall Supper: a fear check DC 15 and, for anyone who does not hide their breath or step onto the wet, one Frost Touch; it does not pursue and does not take anyone

npcsInvolved.name: Elsie Brandvold, 61
npcsInvolved.role: Owner of the Fork Diner; keeper of the motel register; the town's welcome
npcsInvolved.description: Round, quick, warm, sixty-one, in a blue apron, with a memory for every customer's pie. Her husband Arvid bakes. She is the kindest person in Hollow Fork and has written 'checked out' in the register nineteen times.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Arvid's heart attack in 1959 that he should not have survived; the town; and a belief she has had to choose, that the guests go somewhere peaceful.

npcsInvolved.name: Arvid Brandvold, 67
npcsInvolved.description: A big, quiet, floury man who bakes from four in the morning. He makes the bread from co-op flour, the bread that is on every table. He knows what it is for. He waves at strangers through the kitchen window.
npcsInvolved.motivation: He has had fifteen years he was not supposed to have, and he does not let himself think about what paid for them.

npcsInvolved.name: Harald Haugen, 58
npcsInvolved.role: Manager of the co-op; keeper of the Book
npcsInvolved.description: Tall, stooped, grey, careful, with reading glasses on a cord and a good grey suit for church. Polite, generous with the co-op's rooms, and quietly the saddest man in town.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Two hundred and twenty families and a $1.2 million loan, and seventy years of his family's handwriting.

npcsInvolved.name: Rolf Haugen, 24
npcsInvolved.role: Harald's son; drives the co-op grain truck; possible companion
npcsInvolved.description: Big, fair, back two years from the ag school at River Falls, with a CB handle (Little Elevator) and a look of a man who has not slept.
npcsInvolved.motivation: He knows what his father does and has never said so; he is waiting for someone to give him a reason.

npcsInvolved.name: Marit Lunde, 54
npcsInvolved.role: President of the Hollow Fork State Bank
npcsInvolved.description: Trim, silver-haired, tailored, a Buick and a fountain pen; generous with jobs and loans to people she wants to keep close.
npcsInvolved.motivation: A hundred and forty families' notes in her vault.

npcsInvolved.name: Arnie Fossum, 49
npcsInvolved.role: Village president; the biggest farmer; Big Red on channel 14
npcsInvolved.description: Broad, red-faced, laughing, three sons, a new barn and four hundred acres bought on credit.
npcsInvolved.motivation: His land, his boys, his town, in that order, and his debts.

npcsInvolved.name: Lillian Fossum, 46
npcsInvolved.role: Arnie's wife; keeping Dawn; Kitchen Window on channel 14
npcsInvolved.description: Tall, tired, kind, married in from Linden Falls in 1950, which means she was not born here and knows exactly what that means.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Her boys; and terror that one year the board will write her name.

npcsInvolved.name: Dr. Arlen Kubicek, 66
npcsInvolved.description: Small, neat, bow tie, gentle hands. Drops in at the motel to see if anyone needs anything; asks Tess about her nursing. Tells the Fossums Dawn has the flu and needs rest.

npcsInvolved.name: Ingeborg Vaage, 82
npcsInvolved.role: The oldest woman in town; the last witness
npcsInvolved.description: Small, straight-backed, sharp-eyed, gumboots and a cardigan, in the stone house at the rim with a hand pump running at her step.
npcsInvolved.motivation: She watched it begin. She would like to see it end before she dies.

npcsInvolved.name: Pastor Tove Hagstrom, 31
npcsInvolved.role: Pastor of the Community Church since June; possible companion
npcsInvolved.description: A North Dakota farm daughter, the congregation's first woman pastor, warm, funny, lonely, and fed by the town since June.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To do good work in her first parish; she has no idea what the town is, yet.

npcsInvolved.name: Emil Pospisil, 52
npcsInvolved.description: A big, sad, decent man from La Crosse who drives the Madison to Minneapolis run and stops at the Fork Diner twice a week.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Nine years of noticing and not letting himself think about it.

npcsInvolved.name: Bonnie Sedlak, 33
npcsInvolved.description: Sharp, ambitious, a camel coat and a microphone; wants a story she can take to a bigger station.

npcsInvolved.name: Xavier Boone, 29
npcsInvolved.description: A Vietnam combat cameraman with a 16mm Bolex and a .45 in the van's glovebox, quiet, steady, curious.
npcsInvolved.motivation: He filmed the frost line and it frightened him, and he wants to know why.

rewards.money: Nothing changes hands but kindness: free rooms on the co-op, free pie, free bread, and by the end of the week offers of work (Marit Lunde offers Tess a nursing job at Dr. Kubicek's clinic at $4 an hour, Quentin a column in the Furrow, Ward a hauling contract for the co-op at $1.10 a mile). Every one of these is a way of keeping a guest fed and in town. Quentin's paper wires him $50 expenses.
items: A page torn from the motel register, or a Polaroid of it (CLUE A2)
Emil Pospisil's phone number on a diner napkin, and his promise to carry anything out of town
Polaroids or 16mm film of the frost line at the divide (Xavier Boone)
Dawn's yellow cardigan, if Tess takes it from Elsie's kitchen
A red kerchief each, from the co-op store at 39 cents, or from Elsie's nail, free

twists: Russ Thorsen has been eating Elsie's pie once a month for a year. Elsie keeps Unit 3 for him and has his coffee poured before he sits down. He is the most-fed outsider in town, and on Thursday 26 September the board pencils his name under Dawn's in the Book as the alternate. The players will not know this until hs-scenario-002; plant it now with how fond of him everyone is.
The rooms are free 'on the co-op'. Every outsider who stays at the Harvest Moon is on the co-op's books, in the same building as the Book.

Pastor Tove Hagstrom has been the town's guest since June. The town loves her, and the board has discussed her more than once, and has always decided against her because she is too visible. That may change.

Elsie Brandvold is not lying to protect herself. Ask her, gently and alone, whether the young people who stay in Unit 6 go somewhere peaceful, and she will start to cry, and say 'I have to believe that, hon, I have to,' and go into the kitchen. She will not say more this week. She will remember who asked.
dmTips: Ask the players, before the first scene, what they do not want in the game, and honour 'skip that' at any time (dread.json running_horror). This campaign is about a kind town that kills strangers; nobody in it is harmed on the page this week.

Run Hollow Fork warm. The players should like Elsie, Arnie, Ingeborg and Pastor Tove by the end of the session, and want the town to be innocent. The horror is that it is not, and that they understand why.

Track who eats. Every outsider who eats the town's food is a guest (Rule One), and from the second day makes a quiet WIS save each evening (DC 10, +1 per day). Do not make it a mind-control effect: describe a pull, a reluctance, an easy reason to stay; let the player decide. A character who brings their own food and refuses the bread should be noticed, and asked if they are feeling well.

The Harvest Days Clock: say the date every morning in game, and how many days to the festival. On Thursday 26 September the board meets (the party sees six pickups outside the co-op office at seven in the evening and Harald's light on until midnight).

Fear checks this week are small: DC 10 for signs (the register, the frost on the glass, the frost line, the hose), and the first DC 15 for the fog on Main Street. Remember a known rule lowers the DC by 2, and darkness adds 2.

Do not let the party take Dawn this week. If they try, Lillian says she has the flu, Arnie and his sons come out of the barn, Dr. Kubicek arrives, and Dawn herself, drowsy and smiling, says she is fine and is staying for the festival. The town moves to Watchful, and hs-scenario-002 starts with that.
The pregens converge in the diner. If any player wants a reason to trust the others, Elsie gives it to them: she seats all the strangers together, 'so you'll have company'.
Budget an hour for Saturday, an hour for the frost and the TV van, and an hour and a half for Thursday to Sunday, ending on the fog. End the session on the breath.
